name: Swarm Dielectric Dispersal Node SDDN-3 'Locust'
description:
The SDDN-3 deploys a cloud of 400–600 semi-autonomous micro-drones, each no larger than a thumbnail, that distribute themselves across a designated target zone and simultaneously discharge stored dielectric energy into any conductive surface they contact. Each node carries a capacitor array charged via inductive relay from the launch canister, allowing the swarm to sustain its dispersal pattern for up to 90 seconds before terminal discharge. The drones navigate using a low-latency mesh protocol, redistributing around obstacles and reforming after partial neutralization.

What distinguishes the SDDN-3 from conventional area-denial systems is its adaptive saturation logic. If a portion of the swarm is disrupted by EMP countermeasures or physical interference, surviving nodes reassign coverage zones in under 200 milliseconds, ensuring no gap in the dielectric envelope. Targets within the zone experience cascading surface charge buildup across armor, cybernetics, and exposed skin simultaneously, causing localized dielectric breakdown in synthetic materials and severe muscular disruption in unshielded organics.

Originally developed for infrastructure security—specifically to disable unauthorized drones encroaching on TESSERA CORPONATION server campuses—the SDDN-3 was rapidly adopted by paramilitary contractors after field operators discovered its effectiveness against augmented combatants. The swarm's characteristic low hum before dispersal has given it a grim nickname on the streets of GLMZ's industrial districts.
specifications: swarm count: 400–600 micro-drones per canister drone dimensions: 22mm x 14mm x 8mm per unit operational duration: 90 seconds sustained dispersal effective zone radius: 12–18 meters recharge cycle: Inductive relay from launch canister, 4-minute full recharge mesh response latency: <200ms redistribution on node loss canister weight: 2.1 kg power source: Solid-state capacitor array, per-drone countermeasure resistance: Partial EMP tolerance via distributed redundancy
tactical_use: Operators deploy the SDDN-3 into enclosed spaces—corridors, elevator shafts, vehicle bays—ahead of a breach to pre-saturate the zone before entry. The swarm's mesh logic allows it to navigate around cover and reposition under obstacles, making static shielding ineffective. Teams pair the SDDN-3 with hardened armor and insulated cybernetic sleeves. In open terrain, the canister is typically fired via underbarrel launcher at a chokepoint, forcing targets to either push through the swarm or abandon a defensive position. Some operators use partial dispersals to corral targets into kill zones rather than neutralizing them outright.
cultural_context: In GLMZ's corporate security culture, deploying a Locust is considered an escalation signal—it communicates that the operator is not interested in taking prisoners or preserving infrastructure. TESSERA CORPONATION's original marketing positioned the weapon as a 'precision area-denial solution,' but its reputation on the street tells a different story. Mid-tier fixers who can afford the restricted license use SDDN-3 canisters as a status marker, displaying spent housings on their workspace walls. Scavengers prize dead nodes for their miniature capacitor arrays, which have a thriving secondary market in DIY electronics.
known_users: Mid-tier fixers operating in industrial districts
The 'Volt Apostles' gang, known for repurposing scavenged nodes
story_hooks: A spent SDDN-3 canister is found at a crime scene with the TESSERA CORPONATION serial number filed off—someone with corporate access is running unsanctioned operations.
A street-level engineer has reverse-engineered the mesh navigation protocol and is selling modified swarms that ignore corporate IFF signatures, drawing unwanted attention.

The players are hired to clear a building that was hit with an SDDN-3 six months ago—a cluster of nodes went dormant instead of discharging and have been slowly recharging from ambient RF, now nearly at full capacity.

physical_description.visual_profile: A compact, cylindrical launch canister with a distinctly organic, segmented appearance—like a metallic insect thorax. The surface is studded with small inductive relay nodes arranged in a hexagonal pattern. A faint mesh of hairline seams suggests internal compartmentalization. The overall impression is simultaneously mechanical and biomimetic, deliberately evoking the swarm it contains.
physical_description.dimensions: Canister: 18 cm length × 8 cm diameter. Individual drone unit: 22mm × 14mm × 8mm (thumbnail-sized). Launch profile occupies roughly 15 cm when fitted to underbarrel rail.
physical_description.weight_description: Deceptively hefty for its size—2.1 kg of concentrated capacitor density. Feels dense and purposeful in a gloved hand, balanced toward the grip end to distribute recoil evenly during underbarrel deployment.
physical_description.primary_material: Titanium-reinforced polymer casing over a segmented internal lattice of solid-state capacitor arrays. Individual drones use carbon-composite frames with conductive trace routing.
physical_description.finish: Brushed gunmetal-gray anodized titanium, with a subtle matte sheen that minimizes reflectivity. The inductive relay nodes are polished to a high shine, creating deliberate visual contrast.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal gray primary with silver-white inductive relay nodes. Accent striping in electric blue runs along the seams where capacitor segments meet, subtly glowing faint blue under low light when charged.
physical_description.grip_texture: Textured polymer grip panel with fine knurling and integrated palm rest. The junction between canister and grip is wrapped in a thin thermal-dispersal band of braided copper mesh, slightly rough to the touch.
distinctive_features: Hexagonal lattice of inductive relay nodes across the canister surface, each faintly luminous when charged
Linear seam pattern suggesting 12–14 internal capacitor segments, each capable of independent discharge
Threaded underbarrel rail mount with quick-disconnect coupling
Faint QR-scannable manufacturer serial etched on the grip panel
Small red LED status indicator (armed/disarmed state) recessed near the trigger assembly
Faint acoustic dampening grille at the canister tip to muffle the pre-dispersal mesh hum
Micro-ports along the sides—release points for the swarm
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Empathic Analytics corporate sigil (a stylized neural network wrapped around a circle) stamped in raised relief on the grip. Beneath: 'SDDN-3 LOCUST' in sans-serif block letters. Serial number and manufacturing date laser-etched on the underside of the grip panel. Small 'TESSERA CORPORATION' subsidiary logo printed in faded white on the canister body.
physical_description.condition_typical: Usually field-worn but scrupulously maintained. Micro-scratches and scorching on the muzzle end from repeated dispersals. Faint residue of copper oxidation on the relay nodes from inductive cycling. No visible rust or corrosion—standard paramilitary care protocols. Some operators add custom grip tape or engravings, but the SDDN-3's industrial aesthetic resists cosmetic modification.
